Navigation System Architecture

  • •Primary Sensor 

    • –INS or GPS 

  • •Secondary Sensors 

    • –Navigation Aids 

  • •Integration / fusion of all sensor inputs via a Kalman filter in a central computer 

    • –Usually formulated as an error state filter to maximize linearity 

    • –“central computer” could be embedded in primary navigation sensor 

 

Navigation Aids

  • •Velocity Sensors 

    • –Speedometers 

      • •Magnitude of velocity vector in direction of motion 

    • –Doppler Velocity Sensors (DVS) 

      • •Aircraft navigation 

      • •Senses frequency shift of electronmagnetic beam in three directions 

        • –Slaved to body coordinates 

  • •Distance Sensors 

    • –Odometers 

      • •Distance along path traveled 

 

Navigation Aids

  • •Position Fix 

    • –Visual flyover or driveover 

    • –Radar position fix 

      • •Cursor on radar screen initially placed over where the nav computer thinks the target is 

      • •Operator manually corrects by moving cursor to actual target 

      • •Nav computer incorporates deltas as offset corrections 

    • –Altitude Calibration 

      • •Over terrain point of known elevation 

      • •Use radar altimeter to measure distance from aircraft to ground 

      • •Correct for errors in baroaltimeter and INS vertical channel 

 

Navigation Aids

  • •INS 

  • •Attitude Heading Reference System (AHRS) 

    • –Three gyros plus vertical accelerometer 

    • –Possibly magnetic compass input along with magnetic variation tables to correct for gyro drift 

  • •Some experimentation using multiple GPS antennas widely separated 

 

Navigation Aids

  • •Radio Navigation 

    • –VOR:  VHF Omnidirectional Range sensor 

      • •Receiver senses direction of signal (the radial) from external source and computes distance and bearing to external source location 

        • –Intersection of two radials yields a position fix 

      • •DME:  Distance Measuring Equipment 

      • •TACAN:  Tactical Air Navigation = VOR + DME for military (more accurate) 

    • –LORAN-C:  Long Range Navigation 

      • •Time difference of arrival from two sources 

        • –Yields hyperbolic lines of position 

      • •Third source needed to intersect the hyperbolas 

      • •One master station and two secondary stations 

 

LORAN Hyperbolic LOPs

 

Navigation Aids

  • •Satellite Navigation 

    • –Global Positioning System (GPS) 

      • •Six orbital planes, inclined at 55 degrees 

      • •Four or more satellites per orbital plane 

      • •Atomic clocks time tag signals transmitted 

      • •User receivers determine time of flight of signal and computer pseudorange:  R=cΔT to each of the visible satellites 

      • •At least four must be visible to determine position and compensate for receiver clock bias

Navigation Aids

  • •Velocity is calculated using range rate 

  • •GPS Time:  Composite clock of all SV clocks in the constellation 

    • –Steered to within 1 microsecond of UTC, disregarding leap seconds 

 

Navigation Aids:  GPS

  • •Error Sources 

    • –Satellite Clock and Ephemeris Errors 

    • –Ionospheric Delays 

    • –Tropospheric Delays 

    • –Receiver Noise and Resolution 

    • –Multipath 

  • •Dual-Frequency Receivers and Differential GPS can eliminate much of the Ionospheric delay
